title: A Tongue Set on Fire by Gehenna
hook: James says Gehenna sets the tongue on fire now. Is hell a destination or a source?
tldr: James 3:6 is the only New Testament use of Gehenna outside the Gospels, and it sends no one there. Instead Gehenna is the source of a fire burning in the tongue right now, in this life. Drawing on Jewish wisdom about destructive speech, James pictures words that set a whole life ablaze.
big_idea: In James, Gehenna is a fire that reaches into this life.

points.title: The tongue is a fire
points.text: A small spark sets a great forest ablaze. James calls the tongue a fire and a world of iniquity that defiles the whole body and sets the course of life on fire.

points.title: Gehenna as the source
points.text: The tongue 'is set on fire by Gehenna.' Brad Jersak, cited by Jeremy Myers (Redeeming God), argues this shows Gehenna is not where people go after death but the source of flames that burn now.

points.title: The only use outside the Gospels
points.text: Gehenna appears in Jesus' sayings in the Gospels and once more here. James, an early letter by Jesus' half-brother, leans on the Sermon on the Mount, where Jesus links angry words to Gehenna.

points.title: Jewish wisdom on fiery speech
points.text: Proverbs says a worthless man's speech is like scorching fire; Sirach says hasty quarrels kindle fire like pitch and tow. Barnes calls the tongue-as-fire a common Jewish picture.

points.title: Two kingdoms, here and now
points.text: Myers reads hell as a kingdom of darkness and destruction warring against the kingdom of heaven in this life. Its fires are the devastation that comes when we stray from God's ways.

points.title: James 5:3 and the rich
points.text: Corroded gold 'will eat your flesh like fire.' Myers reads this as loss for believers, now and at the Judgment Seat of Christ, where worthless works burn like wood, hay and stubble, not eternal torment.

sections.summary: Jeremy Myers (Redeeming God) notes James is likely one of the earliest New Testament writings, heavily reliant on the Hebrew Scriptures. As a Jerusalem church leader and Jesus' half-brother, James seems to build on the Sermon on the Mount. So his fire and Gehenna imagery helps show how Jesus and the early church used these terms.

James calls the tongue a fire and a world of iniquity among the body's members. It defiles the whole body, sets on fire the course of nature, and is itself set on fire by Gehenna. Clarke took the 'course' or wheel as life's round of miseries, as slanderers make life hard for their targets.

sections.h: The only Gehenna outside the Gospels
sections.summary: Outside Jesus' own sayings, James 3:6 is the only place the New Testament uses Gehenna, which commentators see as James staying close to his Master's teaching. Jesus' first Gehenna saying in Matthew also concerns speech: calling a brother 'fool.' Some versions translate the word 'hell,' others keep 'Gehenna.'

James writes in the tradition of Jewish wisdom. Barnes cites Proverbs 16:27, where a worthless man's speech is like scorching fire, and Sirach 28:11: 'As pitch and tow, so a hasty contention kindleth fire.' Proverbs also says death and life are in the power of the tongue. James later contrasts wisdom from above with earthly wisdom.

Brad Jersak, who wrote the foreword to Myers' book on hell, calls James 3:6 a definitive text: Gehenna is not where people go after death but the source of the flames setting the tongue and the world on fire. Since tongues do not literally burn, the image symbolizes the devastation words cause in a life.

Andrew Perriman notes no one in James is thrown into Gehenna or goes down to it. The phrase looks idiomatic, like Jesus' 'gates of Hades' to Peter. He leaves open whether James means the Gehenna of Jesus' warnings about Jerusalem's destruction or of popular Judaism, calling it a difficult call.

sections.h: The traditional reading: the devil's fire
sections.summary: Older commentators read the phrase as hell's influence. Barnes says 'hell' stands for the devil, as 'heaven' stands for God, and that the tongue's evil takes its origin from hell. Ellicott says the devil uses the tongue to do his damage. Either way, the verse describes a present, active source of evil.

Corroded gold and silver 'will eat your flesh like fire.' Myers notes James writes to brethren and counts the rich among them; reading this as hell would mean losing eternal life through stinginess. He reads it as devastation now and loss at the Judgment Seat of Christ, where hoarded wealth burns like wood, hay and stubble.

sections.h: The kingdom of heaven and the kingdom of hell
sections.summary: Myers sets two kingdoms side by side: everlasting life or death, light or darkness, love or hate, truth or lies, healing or destruction, forgiveness or grudges, revealing or hiding God's image. All are options in this life. Hell is here and now: sickness, abuse, fear, greed, experienced to the degree a person suffers such things.

sections.h: Afterlife-only hell feeds hell on earth
sections.summary: Myers argues that treating hell as only an afterlife experience leaves the present kingdom of hell unchallenged, and that traditional teaching creates psychological hell through fear of God and of loved ones' fate. He urges believers to bring heaven to earth and rescue people from darkness, despair and depression now.

mythfact.myth: James 3:6 warns that sins of the tongue will send you to hell.
mythfact.fact: No one is sent anywhere. The tongue is set on fire by Gehenna: Gehenna is the source of a present fire, not a destination after death.

mythfact.myth: Gehenna is used throughout the New Testament for the afterlife.
mythfact.fact: Outside Jesus' sayings in the Gospels it appears only here, in a verse about speech in this life.

mythfact.myth: James 5:3 says rich people will burn in hell.
mythfact.fact: Myers notes James writes to brethren, including the rich. The fire is devastation now and loss of works at the Judgment Seat of Christ.

quotes.text: The “fire” is not a place of burning and torture in the afterlife, but an experience of death and devastation in this life.
So where is hell? It is here, on this earth. … When is hell? It is now, in our lives.
Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!

verses.role: A small spark sets a great forest ablaze.
The tongue is a fire, set on fire by Gehenna: the source, not destination.
Jesus links contemptuous words to the fire of Gehenna.
A worthless man's speech is like a scorching fire.
Death and life are in the power of the tongue.
'Gates of Hades': a similar idiom, per Perriman.
Corroded wealth eats the flesh like fire: loss for hoarding believers.
Works burned like wood, hay and stubble, yet the person is saved.
All appear before Christ's judgment seat to answer for their deeds.

quiz.q: In James 3:6, what is set on fire by Gehenna?
quiz.why: Gehenna is the source of the tongue's fire. No one is thrown into Gehenna in James.

quiz.q: Where else in the New Testament is Gehenna used?
options: Only in Jesus' sayings in the Gospels
quiz.why: James 3:6 is the only use outside the Gospels, which suggests James is following Jesus' own teaching.

quiz.q: Which Jewish wisdom text compares speech to scorching fire?
quiz.why: Proverbs says a worthless man's speech is like scorching fire; Sirach 28:11 uses a similar image.

objections.claim: James uses Gehenna because the tongue's evil comes from hell itself, the realm of eternal punishment.
objections.strongest: Barnes says 'hell' stands for the devil and the tongue's evil derives its origin from hell. Gehenna in Jesus' mouth meant final judgment, so James assumes that meaning: the tongue is fueled by the very place of damnation.
objections.response: Even on Barnes' reading, the verse describes a present source of evil, not a destination. Barnes himself takes 'hell' to stand for the devil, an influence active now. James never says anyone is thrown into Gehenna. Perriman notes the phrase looks idiomatic, like 'gates of Hades.' Jersak and Myers draw the conclusion: Gehenna here is the source of flames that devastate life now, matching Jewish wisdom's picture of fiery speech.

objections.claim: One idiom in James cannot override Jesus' many Gehenna warnings about being thrown into fire.
objections.strongest: Jesus speaks of the whole body thrown into Gehenna. James' single figurative use tells us little; the Gospels define Gehenna, and they describe a place of punishment.
objections.response: James is the earliest commentary we have on how Jesus' followers used the word, and he uses it of present life. Jesus' own first Gehenna saying concerns words of contempt (Matthew 5:22), the same theme as James 3. Perriman notes Jesus' Gehenna warnings may concern Jerusalem's destruction, and he leaves it open which sense James intends. Either way, neither text describes endless conscious torment.

objections.claim: Calling hell 'here and now' trivializes final judgment and ignores James 5's warnings of coming misery.
objections.strongest: James warns of misery coming on the rich and fire eating their flesh. A present-tense hell removes the urgency of judgment and turns warnings into mere life advice.
objections.response: Myers does not deny future judgment. He reads James 5:3 as a real warning to believers about loss at the Judgment Seat of Christ, where works burn but the person is saved (1 Corinthians 3:14-15). His point is that hell also rules now, in abuse, greed and despair, and that an afterlife-only view leaves Christians ignoring people suffering it today. The urgency increases, not decreases.
